Section II · Anesthetic Physiology · Chapter 11

Neuromuscular Physiology and Pharmacology

Source chapter: J.A. Jeevendra Martyn & Malin Jonsson Fagerlund

A resident reference to the neuromuscular junction: how one nerve impulse becomes a contraction, which receptors are in play, how relaxants and reversal agents act on them, and when the system turns dangerous.

The junction in one view

The nerve packages acetylcholine (ACh) into vesicles, releases it into a narrow cleft, and muscle nicotinic receptors open to depolarize the end plate — every relaxant and reversal agent works by distorting one link in that chain.

Six ideas to carry into the OR

Transmitter

ACh is the natural agonist

It binds nicotinic AChRs on both sides of the cleft — prejunctional and postjunctional.

Two relaxant classes

Agonists vs antagonists

Succinylcholine acts like ACh; nondepolarizing relaxants (NDMRs) block ACh from its binding site.

Dose matters

More drug, more sites

At higher concentrations NDMRs add ion-channel block and prejunctional effects that show up as fade.

Reversal

Two different logics

Neostigmine floods the cleft with ACh; sugammadex encapsulates steroidal relaxants only.

Receptor plasticity

Receptor numbers change

Denervation, burns, sepsis and immobilization upregulate immature and α7 AChRs.

Clinical consequence

Hyperkalemia and resistance

Upregulated receptors mean exaggerated K⁺ release with succinylcholine and resistance to NDMRs.

Principle

Transmission is deliberately over-engineered: far more ACh is released and far more receptors are opened than threshold requires, so a large fraction of receptors must be occupied before weakness appears.

Pearl

Most clinical surprises — fade, resistance, hyperkalemia, prolonged block — are explained by which receptor population is present, not just by the drug dose.

Hazard

Genetic AChR mutations with abnormally slow or fast channel open times can cause a myasthenia-like state even with normal receptor numbers.

Why the classic "single site" model is incomplete
  • Relaxants act prejunctionally as well as postjunctionally.
  • Some relaxants have partial agonist-like actions at the receptor.
  • Relaxants also bind nicotinic and muscarinic receptors outside muscle — carotid body, vagal supply to the heart, bronchial smooth muscle.
  • Disease changes receptor quantity and quality: in myasthenia gravis fewer AChRs means weaker transmission and altered relaxant sensitivity.

Morphology of the junction

Three cells build the synapse — the motor nerve terminal, the muscle fiber and the Schwann cell — and each side is specialized to send or receive a chemical message.

Nerve side

Motor nerve terminal

Loses its myelin at the muscle and sprays into boutons; vesicles cluster at active zones, mitochondria at the back.

Covering

Schwann cell

Caps the terminal; its survival depends on nerve-derived neuregulin, and it maintains the axon.

Muscle side

Folded end plate

Primary and secondary clefts give a very large surface; AChRs sit on the fold shoulders.

Pearl · motor unit

One neuron drives every fiber in its unit, so any agonist acting on the nerve makes the whole unit contract at once — a fasciculation, often visible through skin.

Hazard · extraocular muscle

Multiply innervated, tonic, and carrying mature plus fetal receptors. Succinylcholine gives a contracture of 1–2 minutes with tensions over 12 g per muscle — the authors advise it probably should not be given with open eye injuries.

Human vs rodent junctions; persistence of the end plate
  • Relative to muscle size, human NMJs are smaller than mouse NMJs but have longer folds and deeper gutters.
  • Before birth each fiber has several NMJs; all but one retract at birth.
  • Once formed, the end plate is durable — a replacement nerve reinnervates the same region.
  • Fast-muscle nerve endings are larger and more complex than slow-muscle endings; this may contribute to differing relaxant responses.

The receptor molecule

Architecture

Five-subunit barrel

Pentamer of ~250 kDa, subunits arranged like staves around a central cation pore.

Anchor

Rapsyn, 43 kDa

Cytoplasmic protein that pins each AChR to the end plate in a 1:1 ratio.

Binding site

On the α-subunits

Extracellular site near cysteines at amino acids 192–193; agonists and antagonists compete here.

Lab tool

α-Bungarotoxin

Cobra toxin binding α-subunit residues 185–199; used to count or stain receptors.

How the junction forms and stays mature

Early fetus
Mesodermal myoblasts fuse into multinucleated myotubes; β-integrin needed for fusion and sarcomere assembly.
Innervation
Axons arrive carrying agrin and neuregulins (NRβ-1, NRβ-2).
Clustering
Agrin activates MuSK; scattered AChRs cluster under the nerve with rapsyn and ErbB proteins.
Around birth
γ-containing immature AChRs replaced by ε-containing mature AChRs; ARIA/neuregulin is the leading candidate driver.
Maintenance
Only nuclei under the end plate keep making receptors; nerve-driven electrical activity silences extrajunctional nuclei.
Signaling detail: agrin, MuSK, ErbB and insulin-like pathways
  • Agrin signals through MuSK; neuregulins through ErbB receptors. Together they control both quantity and quality of junctional receptors.
  • Calcitonin gene-related peptide may also help trigger clustering and stabilization.
  • Muscle also releases agrin and neuregulin, but muscle-derived agrin matters less for clustering.
  • Agrin and MuSK also send retrograde signals that shape axon outgrowth and terminal differentiation.
  • Agrin and neuregulin share downstream signals with insulin (e.g., phosphoinositide 3-kinase); loss of this signaling may release immature and α7 AChRs from suppression.
  • Rodents complete extrajunctional repression in ~2 weeks; humans take longer. Mature receptors are linked to the cytoskeleton by integrin, syntrophin, utrophin, dystroglycans and rapsyn.

Nicotinic receptor families at the junction

Three postjunctional isoforms and a prejunctional autoreceptor explain nearly every altered response to relaxants.

Pearl

A conventional AChR is silenced when a single α-subunit is blocked; an α7 receptor with three of its five sites blocked still has two left for an agonist — which is why relaxant resistance tracks α7 expression.

How receptor distribution shifts

A–B · Fetal
Nearly all nuclei make immature and α7 AChRs, spread over the entire fiber.
C · Innervation
Receptors cluster under the nerve; extrasynaptic receptors begin to disappear.
D · Mature
Only ε-receptors, only at the end plate.
E · Disease
γ- and α7-receptors return across the membrane — the substrate for hyperkalemia and NDMR resistance.
Pearl

Malnutrition-related wasting does not induce the immature isoform, unlike inflammatory catabolism.

The wider nicotinic family (Nm vs Nn)
  • 17 vertebrate AChR genes cloned: α1–α10, β1–β4, and one each of γ, δ, ε.
  • γ, δ and ε subunits exist only in muscle. Neurons express only α and β subunits (α2–α10, β2–β4), and these are variants distinct from the muscle genes.
  • Muscle receptors are sometimes labelled Nm; neuronal ones Nn.
  • Neuronal subtypes are found on autonomic ganglia, carotid body chemoreceptor cells (α3, α7, β2 in humans), and immune cells, fibroblasts and chondrocytes (α7).
  • Decamethonium selectively inhibits the muscle receptor; hexamethonium selectively inhibits ganglionic receptors.
  • Some drugs bind only prejunctionally (dihydro-β-erythroidine), others only postjunctionally (α-bungarotoxin).

How drugs act on the junction

Classic block is a competition at the α-subunit; nonclassic block happens in the channel or the receptor's conformation, and does not respond to extra ACh.

Classification explorer · choose a mechanism
Principle

One NDMR molecule silences a receptor, but opening it needs two ACh molecules — so doubling the relaxant concentration demands a fourfold rise in ACh to stay competitive.

Hazard · timing

The molecular basis for not giving an anticholinesterase at deep block: it cannot raise ACh enough to win against a high relaxant concentration.

Pearl · prior succinylcholine

Very rapid desensitization after succinylcholine may explain why a subsequent NDMR seems more potent.

Channel-block drugs and relaxant preferences
  • Channel block may explain neuromuscular effects of antibiotics, cocaine, quinidine, piperocaine, tricyclic antidepressants, naltrexone, naloxone and histrionicotoxin.
  • Pancuronium prefers the recognition site; gallamine (no longer used) acts equally at both sites.
  • Tubocurarine is a pure antagonist at low doses and enters channels at higher doses.
  • Succinylcholine and decamethonium open channels and, being slender, also enter and block them; decamethonium can pass through into the cytoplasm.
  • Whether prolonged ICU NDMR infusion leads to channel occupation is unknown.
Off-target NDMR binding
  • Carotid body: NDMRs blunt the ventilatory response to hypoxia in partially paralyzed humans.
  • Innate immune cells (macrophages, microglia): binding to α7 AChRs may reduce cytokine release.

Calcium, potassium and release

Extracellular Ca²⁺

Small change, big effect

Doubling extracellular Ca²⁺ raises quantal content of the end-plate potential 16-fold; no Ca²⁺, no release.

Posttetanic potentiation

Twitch grows after tetanus

Ca²⁺ accumulates in the terminal during tetanus, so the next twitch releases extra ACh and briefly overcomes the NDMR.

Magnesium

Blocks P channels

Magnesium sulfate for preeclampsia weakens mother and fetus and potentiates relaxants.

L-type blockers

Verapamil, diltiazem, nifedipine

No effect on normal release at therapeutic doses; may slightly deepen NDMR block.

Channel types in the nerve terminal
  • P channels: found only in nerve terminals, sit beside active zones, voltage-dependent; responsible for normal release.
  • L channels: slower; may be recruited during strenuous stimulation to mobilize reserve vesicles.
  • Voltage-gated and Ca²⁺-activated K⁺ channels end terminal depolarization and so limit Ca²⁺ entry.
  • K⁺ channel blockers (4-aminopyridine, tetraethylammonium) prolong the Ca²⁺ current and greatly amplify release.
  • Other bivalent cations (cadmium, manganese) also block P channels.

One impulse, step by step

Follow a single nerve action potential from calcium entry to muscle membrane firing — each step is a target for a drug, toxin or disease.

Step 1 of 4

Synthesis and the calcium trigger

  • Choline is transported in; acetyl CoA comes from mitochondria; choline acetyltransferase joins them into ACh.
  • Choline uptake and CAT activity are probably rate-limiting.
  • The action potential opens voltage-gated P-type Ca²⁺ channels lined up beside the active zones.
  • Release follows within 200 µs — Ca²⁺ travels only a few atomic radii to reach a vesicle.
Disease link

Eaton–Lambert syndrome: antibodies against these Ca²⁺ channels reduce release and increase sensitivity to both relaxant classes.

Step 2 of 4

Docking and exocytosis

  • Ca²⁺ phosphorylates synapsin, freeing the vesicle from the cytoskeleton.
  • Vesicle synaptobrevin locks with membrane syntaxin and SNAP-25 into a ternary complex.
  • Synaptotagmin, the Ca²⁺ sensor, holds the vesicle docked in Ca²⁺-rich zones.
  • Each impulse releases ≥200 quanta of ~5000 ACh molecules.
Vesicle pools and recycling
  • Readily releasable pool: small vesicles bound at active zones — the ones used normally.
  • Reserve pool: larger, deeper, tethered by actin, synapsin, synaptotagmin and spectrin; recruited during hard repetitive stimulation (mobilization).
  • After fusion a vesicle may reclose quickly ("kiss and run"), stay open longer ("compensatory"), or collapse fully and wait for the next stimulus ("stranded").
  • Spontaneous single-quantum release produces miniature end-plate potentials (MEPPs) — about one hundredth of the evoked potential.
Step 3 of 4

Receptor activation

  • ACh must occupy both α-subunits; one molecule is not enough.
  • The receptor twists open: Na⁺ and Ca²⁺ flow in, K⁺ flows out; anions such as Cl⁻ are excluded.
  • Each open channel passes only a few picoamperes, but ~500,000 open together.
  • The end-plate potential is the sum of many all-or-nothing channel events.
  • Unbound ACh is hydrolysed by acetylcholinesterase in <1 ms; each molecule normally meets only one receptor.
Pearl

Channels can also flicker, open slowly, or pass more or fewer ions — temperature, electrolytes, membrane fluidity and drugs all shift these states.

Step 4 of 4

Firing the muscle membrane

  • The end-plate potential opens voltage gates of perijunctional Na⁺ channels, launching a wave of depolarization along the fiber.
  • Na⁺ flows only when both gates are open; the time gate soon closes.
  • Three states in sequence: resting → open → inactivated.
  • With ACh this cycle is brief, and the end plate resets before the next impulse.
Why succinylcholine blocks

It persists, so the end plate stays depolarized, perijunctional Na⁺ channels are frozen inactivated and the nerve's next burst of ACh cannot get through — accommodation.

Pearl

Direct electrical stimulation of muscle still produces contraction during a depolarizing block, because the Na⁺ channels beyond the perijunctional buffer zone are resting and excitable.

Succinylcholine hyperkalemia

When immature and α7 receptors cover the whole muscle surface, systemic succinylcholine opens all of them at once and potassium pours out.

Upregulating states

  • Upper or lower motor neuron denervation
  • Stroke
  • Burns
  • Sepsis / generalized inflammation
  • Immobilization
  • Chronic NDMR therapy
  • Botulism
  • Loss of muscle electrical activity
Hours
Immature receptor synthesis begins after inactivity.
Several days
Whole membrane covered with receptors.
Beyond 72 h
Relaxant sensitivity starts to change.
Hazard · pretreatment fails

Prior NDMR cannot reliably prevent it: a dose large enough to block the receptors would itself paralyze. Larger doses only blunt the K⁺ rise.

Hazard · no denervation needed

Some congenital muscular dystrophies release K⁺ through membrane damaged by succinylcholine depolarization, with cardiac arrest possible.

Principle

The same receptor shift produces two opposite errors: exaggerated sensitivity to succinylcholine and resistance to nondepolarizing relaxants — and it may be confined to the affected muscles, as after a stroke.

Mechanisms of NDMR resistance
  • Junctional α7 expression with low NDMR affinity — currently the favored explanation (absent in α7-knockout mice).
  • Some NDMRs act as partial agonists on immature receptors.
  • Extra perijunctional and extrajunctional receptors may buffer relaxant diffusion.
  • Electrical stimulation of denervated muscle can prevent immature receptor appearance; Ca²⁺ entry during activity seems important for suppression.
  • These receptor changes are potentially reversible when immobilization, catabolism and inflammation resolve.

Disorders along the chain

Prejunctional · Ca²⁺ channel

Eaton–Lambert syndrome

Autoantibodies cut transmitter release; increased sensitivity to depolarizing and nondepolarizing relaxants.

Prejunctional · SNARE

Clostridial toxins

Botulinum digests SNAREs — partial or complete chemical denervation; systemic paralysis possible after infection.

Prejunctional · Mg²⁺

Preeclampsia therapy

Magnesium reduces ACh release — weakness in mother or newborn.

Cleft · enzyme

Cholinesterase disorders

Congenital absence or chronic inhibition (organophosphates, sarin, prophylactic pyridostigmine) causes fatigue to weakness.

Postjunctional · number

Myasthenia gravis

Fewer AChRs lower the margin of safety, cause fade and alter relaxant sensitivity.

Postjunctional · gating

Slow- and fast-channel syndromes

Mutated receptors with abnormal open times give a myasthenia-like state.

More on botulinum toxin and cholinesterase disease

Botulinum

  • Heavy chain binds polysialogangliosides and synaptotagmin to enter; the light chain then cleaves SNARE proteins.
  • Infection is particularly common after traumatic injuries, in drug users, and after musculoskeletal allografts.
  • Therapeutic uses: spasticity and spasm, hyperhidrosis, cosmetic wrinkle correction; local injection usually gives local paresis but systemic effects are reported.

Acetylcholinesterase

  • Junctional enzyme is the asymmetric A12 form, made by muscle under the end plate; a type B carboxylesterase.
  • Congenital absence impairs maintenance of the motor system and terminal branching; many congenital syndromes mimic myasthenia.
  • Denervation reduces enzyme both junctionally and extrajunctionally.
  • In rodents, weakness from chronic pyridostigmine reflects AChR downregulation plus receptor-independent factors.

Fade and the prejunctional receptor

Positive feedback

α3β2 autoreceptor

Senses ACh in the cleft and boosts further release; blocked by all clinical NDMRs.

NDMR

Fade on TOF and tetanus

Combined pre- and postjunctional block reduces release on repeated stimulation.

Succinylcholine

Usually no fade

Neither activates nor inhibits α3β2 at clinical concentrations.

Pearl

Fade needs more than prejunctional block — a reduced safety margin pre- or postjunctionally must also be present. Fade also appears with bungarotoxin block or low receptor numbers (myasthenia).

Fasciculations and phase II block
  • Only the nerve can synchronize a whole motor unit, so succinylcholine fasciculations prove a prejunctional action; NDMRs prevent them by occupying the same nerve-terminal receptor.
  • Phase II block is fade during continued exposure to a depolarizer, partly from succinylcholine acting on prejunctional neuronal AChRs at higher concentrations.
  • Its development depends on exposure time, drug, concentration, muscle type (fast vs slow) and interacting anesthetics.
  • It is not simply "desensitization block" — desensitization is one of several contributors.
  • The existence of α3β2 prejunctionally has not been confirmed by Western blot or mRNA methods.
  • The terminal also carries opioid, adrenergic, dopamine, purine and adenosine receptors, whose roles and anesthetic interactions are unknown.

Extremes of age

Newborn

Behaves like myasthenia

Few folds, wide cleft, fewer AChRs — neonates and infants respond to NDMRs as myasthenic patients do.

Maturation

About 2 years

The human NMJ probably matures at approximately 2 years of age.

Old age

Denervation-like, still safe

Sarcopenia and junction degeneration, yet the safety margin exceeds the neonate's.

What the evidence does and does not show in the elderly
  • Functional changes: higher quantal content and faster rundown of end-plate potential during repetitive stimulation.
  • Deficits are rarely detectable by simple tests such as grip strength.
  • No evidence of increased succinylcholine hyperkalemia risk; in frailty the denervation state is exaggerated.
  • No studies confirm altered NDMR sensitivity from NMJ changes; some agents (e.g., vecuronium) last longer for pharmacokinetic reasons.
Source: Martyn JAJ, Fagerlund MJ. Chapter 11, Neuromuscular Physiology and Pharmacology. Section II: Anesthetic Physiology, pp. 225–244.
